l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone grieves for thou
q: What joy have I in life when thou art gone?

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Eteocles' burial honors Eteocles (through burial rites and libations)
q: Then nimbly with her hands she brought dry dust, And holding high a shapely brazen cruse, Poured three libations, honouring the dead.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon is father of Haemon
q: O my sire,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Mankind is inventive boundless skill (in overcoming difficulties)
q: Inventive beyond wildest hope, endowed with boundless skill,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon is uncle of Antigone (through his sister)
q: Be she my sister's child, Or of yet nearer blood to me than all That take protection from my hearth, the pair Shall not escape the worst of deaths.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon issues the law (forbidding burial of the enemy)
q: Knew'st thou our edict that forbade this thing?

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon will take life her
q: I will take her life.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon's death sentence against Antigone confines Antigone (alive in a cave-like tomb)
q: I'll hide her living in a cave like vault, With so much provender as may prevent Pollution from o'ertaking the whole city

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Haemon is a son of Creon
q: O my sire,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Haemon pleads against the unreason of your fault
q: I plead against the unreason of your fault.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Haemon values Antigone (for her burial of her brother)
q: Who, when her own true brother on the earth Lay weltering after combat in his gore, Left him not graveless, for the carrion few And raw devouring field dogs to consume-- Hath she not merited a golden praise

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Ismene is sister of Antigone
q: What joy have I in life when thou art gone?

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Ismene is cautious prudence (in contrast with Antigone's defiance)
q: I warned thee----

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Mankind subdues Earth (through cultivation and labor)
q: And Earth, supreme of mighty Gods, eldest, imperishable, Eternal, he with patient furrow wears and wears away As year by year the plough-shares turn and turn,-- Subduing her unwearied strength with children of the steed[4].

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Chorus of Theban Elders is maze with doubt and fear
q: What portent from the Gods is here? My mind is mazed with doubt and fear.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: the Gods publish the law
q: I heard it not from Heaven, nor came it forth From Justice, where she reigns with Gods below. They too have published to mankind a law.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: the Gods inflict human suffering and inherited doom (upon the house of Cadmus)
q: When once the blow Hath fallen upon a house with Heaven-sent doom, Trouble descends in ever-widening gloom Through all the number of the tribe to flow;

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Death is a deity (Antigone's only deity in the tomb)
q: And there, perchance, she may obtain of Death, Her only deity, to spare her soul,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Thebes is a city (governed by Creon)
q: One only makes not up a city, father.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: the people of Thebes approve Eteocles' burial (but fear to speak openly under Creon's rule)
q: All here would tell thee they approve my deed, Were they not tongue-tied to authority.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: the people of Thebes oppose Creon's death sentence against Antigone (quietly and through rumor)
q: I under shadow may o'erhear, how all Thy people mourn this maiden, and complain That of all women least deservedly She perishes for a most glorious deed.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: the law is a unwritten law of Heaven (infallible and everlasting)
q: Nor thought I thy commandment of such might That one who is mortal thus could overbear The infallible, unwritten laws of Heaven. Not now or yesterday they have their being, But everlastingly, and none can tell The hour that saw their birth.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: human suffering and inherited doom afflicts the stock of Cadmus (across successive generations)
q: The stock of Cadmus from old time, I know, I 2 Hath woe on woe, Age following age, the living on the dead, Fresh sorrow falling on each new-ris'n head

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: the cave-like tomb contains Antigone (alive and provisioned)
q: I'll hide her living in a cave like vault, With so much provender as may prevent Pollution from o'ertaking the whole city

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Mankind controls the sea (by sailing across it)
q: That courseth over the grey ocean, carried of Southern gale, Faring amidst high-swelling seas that rudely surge around,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Mankind captures wild animals (with nets and devices)
q: And wound in woven coils of nets he seizeth for his prey I 2 The aëry tribe of birds and wilding armies of the chase, And sea-born millions of the deep--man is so crafty-wise

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Mankind tames wild beasts (with yokes and harness)
q: And now with engine of his wit he tameth to his will The mountain-ranging beast whose lair is in the country wild; And now his yoke hath passed upon the mane Of horse with proudly crested neck and tireless mountain bull.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Mankind possesses wise utterance and wind-swift thought
q: Wise utterance and wind-swift thought, and city-moulding mind,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Mankind creates cures for disease (even for diseases baffling physicians)
q: but even for fell disease, That long hath baffled wisest leech, he hath contrived a cure.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Mankind cannot escape Death
q: From Death alone he shall not find reprieve;

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone is a daughter of Oedipus
q: Thy father's lot still presseth hard on thee.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon is a ruler of Thebes
q: Know'st thou 'tis of thy sovereign thou speak'st this?

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon orders Antigone's burial (as punishment)
q: Away with her at once, and closing her, As I commanded, in the vaulty tomb, Leave her all desolate, whether to die, Or to live on in that sepulchral cell.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon issues Creon's proclamation against Polynices' burial (forbidding burial of Polynices)
q: No, not if heaven's own eagle chose to snatch And bear him to the throne supreme for food, Even that pollution should not daunt my heart To yield permission for his funeral.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon is waited for by the avengers
q: Such violence the powers beneath will bear Not even from the Olympian gods. For thee The avengers wait.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon reverses Creon's proclamation against Polynices' burial (after Tiresias' prophecy)
q: Go and release the maiden from the vault, And make a grave for the unburied dead.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Tiresias is blind blind (in frail dependence on a guide)
q: We are come, my lords of Thebes, joint wayfarers, One having eyes for both. The blind must still Thus move in frail dependence on a guide.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Tiresias is guided by Tiresias' guide (because he is blind)
q: The blind must still Thus move in frail dependence on a guide.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Tiresias foretells Tiresias' prophecy (to Creon)
q: Not many courses of the racing sun Shalt thou fulfil, ere of thine own true blood Thou shalt have given a corpse in recompense

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Tiresias' prophecy foretells Creon's ruin (as punishment for his actions)
q: For thee The avengers wait. Hidden but near at hand, Lagging but sure, the Furies of the grave Are watching for thee to thy ruinous harm,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone is a sister of Polynices
q: O brother mine, thy princely marriage-tie Hath been thy downfall, and in this thy death Thou hast destroyed me ere I die.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Chorus of Theban Elders urges Creon (to obey Tiresias' warning)
q: The time calls loud on wisdom, good my lord. CR. What must I do? Advise me. I will obey. CH. Go and release the maiden from the vault, And make a grave for the unburied dead.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Thebes is a city (ancestral city of Antigone)
q: O land of Thebè, city of my sires, Ye too, ancestral Gods! I go--I go!

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Thebes is polluted by Polynices' corpse (through the desecration of his unburied body)
q: Such failing tokens of blurred augury This youth reported, who is guide to me, As I to others. And this evil state Is come upon the city from thy will: Because our altars--yea, our sacred hearths-- Are everywhere infected from the mouths Of dogs or beak of vulture that hath fed On Oedipus' unhappy slaughtered son

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Polynices is a son of Oedipus (slaughtered in battle)
q: On Oedipus' unhappy slaughtered son.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Polynices' corpse lacks burial (by Creon's order)
q: And one whom thou hast kept above the ground And disappointed of all obsequies, Unsanctified and godlessly forlorn.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: the Gods refuse sacrifice (because of pollution)
q: And then at sacrifice the Gods refuse Our prayers and savour of the thigh-bone fat

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Fate overcomes mortals (irresistibly)
q: Fated misfortune hath a power so fell: Not wealth, nor warfare wild, Nor dark spray-dashing coursers of the main Against great Destiny may once rebel.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone is a last scion of Cadmus' issue
q: Founders of Thebes, the only scion left Of Cadmus' issue, how unworthily, By what mean instruments I am oppressed,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: death is a silent strand (the destination of the condemned)
q: Led my last path toward the silent strand. Alive to the wide house of rest I go;

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: the cave-like tomb is a vaulty tomb (sepulchral prison-house)
q: O grave! my bridal chamber, prison-house Eterne, deep-hollowed, whither I am led

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone's burial is ordered by Creon (as confinement alive in a tomb)
q: Away with her at once, and closing her, As I commanded, in the vaulty tomb,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Furies pursue Creon (as avengers of the dead)
q: For thee The avengers wait. Hidden but near at hand, Lagging but sure, the Furies of the grave Are watching for thee to thy ruinous harm,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone is unmarried no marriage (when led to the tomb)
q: Unmourned, they lead me on my destined way. Woe for my life forlorn! I may not see The sacred round of yon great light Rising again to greet me from the night; No friend bemoans my fate, no tear hath fallen for me!

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone has no children no children
q: For neither, had I children, nor if one I had married were laid bleeding on the earth,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone honours Polynices (by tending his corpse)
q: And I reap this doom For tending, Polynices, on thy corse. Indeed I honoured thee, the wise will say.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone is pious Justice
q: For what transgression of Heaven's ordinance? Alas! how can I look to Heaven? on whom Call to befriend me? seeing that I have earned, By piety, the meed of impious?

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone is condemned to death (by Creon's decree)
q: Alive to the wide house of rest I go; No dawn for me may shine,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone is confined in the cave-like tomb (alive)
q: I go to the strong mound of yon strange tomb,-- All hapless, having neither part nor room With those who live or those who die!

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Bacchus is a god
q: O God of many a name!

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: second Messenger addresses my lord and master (master here)
q: My lord and master. Thou art master here Of nought but sorrows.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon is a king (of Thebè)
q: Ah! look where sadly comes our lord the King,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon rules Thebes (with supreme authority and formerly aright)
q: Creon erewhile to me was enviable, Who saved our Thebè from her enemies; Then, vested with supreme authority, Ruled her aright;

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon is father of Haemon
q: O ye who now behold Slayer and slain of the same kindred blood! O bitter consequence of seeming-wise decree! Alas, my son!

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon is husband of Eurydicè
q: The honoured mother of that corse, thy queen, Is dead, and bleeding with a new-given wound.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon issues Creon's proclamation against Polynices' burial (a seemingly wise but ruinous decree)
q: O bitter consequence of seeming-wise decree!

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon causes Haemon's death (through his treatment of Antigone)
q: his father's crime And his lost love

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon is denounced by this dead lady (for the guilt of this and the former grief)
q: The guilt of this and of the former grief By this dead lady was denounced on thee.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon is guilty of the death of Antigone (through the murder of the maid)
q: At Creon for the murder of the maid.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Bacchus is child of Semele
q: Thou and the nymph whom lightning made Mother of thy radiant head.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon recognizes his folly (too late)
q: I have learnt it now.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Eurydicè is a queen (of Thebè)
q: The honoured mother of that corse, thy queen, Is dead, and bleeding with a new-given wound.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Eurydicè is mother of Haemon
q: The honoured mother of that corse, thy queen,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Eurydicè dies by Eurydice's suicide (after hearing of Haemon's death)
q: Wounding herself to the heart, when she had heard The loud lamented death of Haemon here.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Eurydicè pronounces the curse of murdered offspring (against Creon before dying)
q: And then of Haemon; lastly clamoured forth The curse of murdered offspring upon thee

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Haemon is a son (of Creon)
q: O bitter consequence of seeming-wise decree! Alas, my son!

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Haemon is betrothed to Antigone (in a nuptial union completed by death)
q: Lamenting o'er his ruined nuptial-rite, Consummated in death, his father's crime And his lost love.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Haemon dies by Haemon's death (by his own sword)
q: the unhappy boy, Wroth with himself, even where he stood, leant heavily Upon his sword and plunged it in his side.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Haemon is found with Antigone (dead in the burial vault)
q: And clinging to her on his knees the boy, Lamenting o'er his ruined nuptial-rite,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone is a maiden (confined in a stone death-chamber)
q: The maiden's stony bride-chamber of death.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Bacchus presides over Dêo (in the all-gathering bosom)
q: Thou for Italia's good Dost care, and 'midst the all-gathering bosom wide[7] Of Dêo dost preside;

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone dies by the death of Antigone (by hanging)
q: We saw the maiden hanging by the neck With noose of finest tissue firmly tied

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone dies by hanging noose of finest tissue (firmly tied)
q: We saw the maiden hanging by the neck With noose of finest tissue firmly tied,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Thebes is a city (first among cities)
q: For Thebè thou dost still uphold, II 1 First of cities manifold

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Thebes is saved by Creon (from its enemies)
q: Who saved our Thebè from her enemies;

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: the burial vault contains Antigone (as her stone death-chamber)
q: Then we turned us to the vault, The maiden's stony bride-chamber of death.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Haemon's corpse is carried by Creon (in Creon's arms)
q: Ah! look where sadly comes our lord the King, Bearing upon his arm a monument-- If we may speak it--of no foreign woe, But of his own infirmity the fruit.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Eurydice's suicide is caused by Haemon's death (after she hears the lamented death)
q: Wounding herself to the heart, when she had heard The loud lamented death of Haemon here.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: rashness is a evil (the worst evil in mortal life)
q: A monument unto mankind, that rashness Is the worst evil of this mortal state.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Bacchus haunts Thebes (among the frenzied daughters of Thebes)
q: Thou, Bacchus, by Ismenus' winding waters 'Mongst Thebè's frenzied daughters, Keep'st haunt, commanding the fierce dragon's brood.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: pride is punished by sorrow (when it is boastful and excessive)
q: High boastings of the proud Bring sorrow to the height to punish pride:

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: piety toward the gods must be preserved by human beings (as a condition of wise conduct)
q: Wise conduct hath command of happiness Before all else, and piety to Heaven Must be preserved.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: human happiness and woe is governed by Fortune (as Fortune smiles or lowers)
q: human happiness and human woe Come even as fickle Fortune smiles or lours

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Fate determines human suffering (through its own dread work)
q: Time will determine that. We must attend To present needs. Fate works her own dread work.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Bacchus is honoured by Bacchae (with cries of Evoe)
q: While myriad voices sound Loud strains of 'Evoe!' to thy deathless praise.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Bacchus moves over Nyseian height (over the ivy-mantled mound)
q: To visit Theban ways, By bloomy wine-cliffs flushing tender bright 'Neath far Nyseian height Thou movest o'er the ivy-mantled mound,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Bacchus is leader of Thyiads (in their night-long procession)
q: Come, leader of the starry quire II 2 Quick-panting with their breath of fire! Lord of high voices of the night, Child born to him who dwells in light, Appear with those who, joying in their madness, Honour the sole dispenser of their gladness, Thyiads of the Aegean main Night-long trooping in thy train

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Athena guards Odysseus (during his pursuit of Aias)
q: I knew thy doubts, Odysseus, and came forth Zealous to guard thy perilous hunting-path.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias guards Salamis (whose hand)
q: Telamonian child, whose hand Guards our wave-encircled land, Salamis that breasts the sea

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias is valiant Greeks (most valiant of the surviving Greeks)
q: Although Aias was the most valiant, the judges made the award to Odysseus, because he was the wisest.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias loses honour (after the award of Achilles' armour to Odysseus)
q: On awakening from his delusion, he finds that he has fallen irrecoverably from honour and from the favour of the Greeks.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias experiences Aias's madness (divinely imposed)
q: Athena sends madness upon him, and he makes a raid upon the flocks and herds of the army

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias attempts to attack the generals (in rage over Achilles' armour)
q: Aias in his rage attempts to kill the generals

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias raids the flocks and herds (mistaking them for the Argive chiefs)
q: he makes a raid upon the flocks and herds of the army, imagining the bulls and rams to be the Argive chiefs.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias wields the sword (Aias's sword gifted by Hector) (during the slaughter of the livestock)
q: seizing his sharp blade, He sought on some vain errand to creep forth.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias is betrothed to Tecmessa (captive-bride relationship)
q: Since Aias, foremost in the fray, Disdaining not the spear-won bride, Still holds thee nearest at his side

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias has as child Eurysakes (child of Aias and Tecmessa)
q: EURYSAKÈS, _the child of Aias and Tecmessa, appears, but does not speak._

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Athena causes Aias's madness (to prevent the killing of the Argive leaders)
q: I turned him backward from his baleful joy, And overswayed him with blind phantasies, To swerve against the flocks and well-watched herd

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias dies by the sword (Aias's sword gifted by Hector) (after the return of his reason)
q: and falls on his sword.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias receives Aias' funeral (after Teucer and Odysseus overcome the Atreidae's opposition)
q: on the return of Teucer, Aias receives an honoured funeral

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Tecmessa is a captive-bride (of Aias)
q: Since Aias, foremost in the fray, Disdaining not the spear-won bride, Still holds thee nearest at his side

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Tecmessa is daughter of Teleutas (Phrygian lineage)
q: Phrygian Teleutas' daughter, say;

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Tecmessa has as child Eurysakes (with Aias)
q: EURYSAKÈS, _the child of Aias and Tecmessa, appears, but does not speak._

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Salaminian Mariners is a chorus (of Aias's sailors)
q: CHORUS _of Salaminian Mariners._

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Achilles' armour is made by Hephaestus (divine craftsmanship)
q: the armour made for him by Hephaestus

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Athena protects Aias (from his own intended attack on the generals)
q: Planned, and performed, had I kept careless guard.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: the prize-encounter for Pelides' arms determines Odysseus (as recipient of Achilles' armour)
q: Although Aias was the most valiant, the judges made the award to Odysseus, because he was the wisest.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias's madness is caused by Athena (as divine intervention)
q: Athena sends madness upon him

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias's madness causes Aias' raid on the army's livestock (through delusion)
q: Athena sends madness upon him, and he makes a raid upon the flocks and herds of the army

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias' raid on the army's livestock targets the flocks and herds (belonging to the army)
q: he makes a raid upon the flocks and herds of the army

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias' raid on the army's livestock is mistaken for Aias' attempted attack on the generals (in Aias's delusion)
q: imagining the bulls and rams to be the Argive chiefs.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias' attempted attack on the generals is prevented by Athena (through divine madness)
q: I turned him backward from his baleful joy, And overswayed him with blind phantasies

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: honour is lost by Aias (after his delusion and livestock slaughter)
q: he has fallen irrecoverably from honour and from the favour of the Greeks.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Athena inspires Odysseus (to accept Aias's funeral)
q: the magnanimity of Odysseus, who has been inspired for this purpose by Athena.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: honour is restored to Aias (through his honoured funeral)
q: Aias receives an honoured funeral

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Odysseus is a Laërtiades (Greek commander)
q: ATHENA. Oft have I seen thee, Laërtiades,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Odysseus undertakes this toil (to determine if he did this thing)
q: For he hath wrought on us to night a deed Past thought--if he be doer of this thing; We drift in ignorant doubt, unsatisfied-- And I unbidden have bound me to this toil.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Odysseus pities Aias (despite their enmity)
q: But, though he hates me sore, I pity him, poor mortal, thus chained fast To a wild and cruel fate

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Odysseus is opposed to Aias (as a hostile rival)
q: He was and is my valiant enemy.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias is a son of Telamon (Greek warrior)
q: AIAS, _the son of Telamon._

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias has achievements the achievements of my hand (not less of might than he)
q: But I his son, not less of might than he, Nor poorer in the achievements of my hand, To this same region following in my prime,

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias possesses Aias's seven-hided shield (intended for Eurysakes)
q: But thou, named of the shield[3], Eurysakes, hold mine, the unpierceable Seven-hided buckler, and by the well stitched thong Grasp firm and wield it mightily.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias contemplates Aias's contemplated suicide (as an escape from dishonor)
q: Shame on the wight who when beset with ill Cares to live on in misery unrelieved. Can hour outlasting hour make less or more Of death? Whereby then can it furnish joy?

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias is shorn of all that pride
q: Now, shorn of all that pride, I lie thus low.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias is honored as greatest Greek warrior (before his disgrace)
q: One, I will vaunt it forth! Highest in warlike worth Of all Greek forms that Troia's towers have eyed: Now, shorn of all that pride, I lie thus low.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Tecmessa is a captive woman (formerly free and of noble Phrygian birth)
q: I, born of one the mightiest of the free And wealthiest in the Phrygian land, am now A captive.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Tecmessa is taken with thy boy (if thou die)
q: For, shouldst thou die and leave us, then shall I Borne off by Argive violence with thy boy Eat from that day the bread of slavery.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Antigone tells Ismene that Creon has ordered Eteocles buried with full honors but has forbidden burial and mourning for Polynices. Antigone declares that she will bury Polynices despite the order, while Ismene refuses to join her because they are women subject to authority and lack the strength to oppose the citizens. Creon announces his policy of honoring those loyal to Thebes and punishing disobedience, and a watchman reports that Polynices’ corpse has been covered with dust and given burial rites. Creon rejects the suggestion of divine intervention and orders the watchmen to find the person responsible.

l: Antigone, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Antigone tells Ismene that Creon has forbidden Polynices’ burial and asks her to share the danger and labor of burying him. She declares that she will bury her brother alone, valuing duty toward the dead above pleasing men and accepting the possibility of death.

l: Ismene, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Ismene refuses to join Antigone in burying Polynices, arguing that they are women who must submit to stronger authority and that they cannot withstand the citizens’ resolve. She agrees to keep Antigone’s plan secret, though Antigone rejects secrecy.

l: Creon, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Creon, newly ruling Thebes, declares that Eteocles will receive full burial honors while Polynices will remain unburied. He insists that loyalty to the state must come before friendship and threatens death for anyone who disobeys his order.

l: Polynices, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Polynices is described as having returned against Thebes with an Argive army and as having fought against his native city. Creon condemns him as an enemy of Thebes and denies him mourning and funeral rites.

l: Eteocles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Eteocles is described as having fought for Thebes and died in single combat with Polynices. Creon orders that he be entombed with the sacred rites and honors due to a distinguished dead man.

l: Chorus of Theban Elders, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: The Chorus celebrates Thebes’ victory over the Argive attack and laments the mutual deaths of Polynices and Eteocles. It acknowledges Creon’s authority but suggests that a divine power may have caused Polynices’ body to receive burial.

l: Theban citizens, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Theban citizens are subject to Creon’s order and are threatened with stoning if they disobey it. Creon also speaks of malcontents among them who resent his rule.

l: watchmen, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: The watchmen discover that Polynices’ corpse has been covered with dust and given the required religious rites. They argue among themselves, fear punishment, and are ordered by Creon to find the person who performed the burial.

l: Thebes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Thebes is celebrated as having survived the Argive attack and is personified as victorious and restored to peace. Creon presents its safety and greatness as the chief concern of his rule.

l: Creon's proclamation against Polynices' burial, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Creon’s proclamation forbids anyone to cover Polynices’ body, mourn him, or give him funeral rites. It declares that his corpse must remain exposed to carrion birds and dogs, and that anyone who disobeys will be killed.

l: the attack on Thebes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: The attack on Thebes is described as an Argive assault intended to destroy the city, burn its shrines, and capture its people. Thebes defeats the attackers, who flee after their leaders are overcome.

l: the deaths of Polynices and Eteocles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Polynices and Eteocles kill each other in single combat after the conflict between Thebes and Argos. Their mutual death ends the struggle between the two brothers.

l: Polynices' burial, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Polynices receives burial from an unidentified person despite Creon’s prohibition. The burial consists of dust placed over his body and the religious rites required for the dead.

l: Antigone's disobedience, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Antigone openly resolves to disobey Creon’s command by burying Polynices. In this unit, the watchman reports that the burial has occurred, but he does not identify the person who performed it.

l: the conflict between Eteocles and Polynices, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: The war between Thebes and Argos is described as an Argive invasion led by Polynices against his native city. The Argive army is defeated, and the conflict results in the deaths of Polynices and Eteocles.

l: burial rites, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Creon grants Eteocles the full sacred rites appropriate to an honored dead man while denying them to Polynices. The watchman reports that someone has nevertheless performed the required rites for Polynices.

l: loyalty to the state, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Creon declares that loyalty to the state must take precedence over personal friendship. He promises honor in life and death to those who love Thebes and denies recognition to those he considers enemies.

l: Justice, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Antigone appeals to laws revered on high and places her duty toward the dead above Creon’s command. The Chorus suggests that a divine power may have intervened in Polynices’ burial, but Creon rejects this interpretation.

l: authority and obedience, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Ismene argues that obedience to authority is necessary because she and Antigone are women and lack power to resist the citizens and the king. Creon demands obedience to his decree and threatens severe punishment for disobedience.

l: Polynices' corpse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: Polynices’ corpse is found outside a grave, with no signs that animals have touched it. It has been covered with a thin layer of dust and treated with the rites required for burial.

l: dust covering Polynices' body, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: A thin layer of dust has been placed over Polynices’ body by someone who left no identifiable trace. The dust is presented as part of the burial act that violates Creon’s order.

l: grave, The Seven Plays in English Verse, ANTIGONE
s: The watchman reports that Polynices is not in a grave. Instead, the body lies with dust covering it and with the required religious rites performed.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Antigone is caught burying the dead body of Eteocles despite Creon's edict and openly defends her action by appealing to the unwritten laws of Heaven. Creon sentences Antigone to be shut alive in a cave-like tomb, rejecting appeals from Antigone, Ismene, the Chorus, and Haemon. Ismene tries to share Antigone's guilt, but Antigone refuses to let her claim a deed she did not perform. Haemon argues that Thebes disapproves of Antigone's punishment, but he leaves in anger when Creon refuses to change his decision.

l: Mankind, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus praises man as a creature of extraordinary skill who masters the sea, earth, animals, birds, fish, language, thought, cities, shelter, and medicine. Yet man cannot escape Death, and his resourcefulness may lead either toward good or toward evil.

l: Antigone, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Antigone admits that she buried the dead body of Eteocles despite Creon's prohibition. She declares that the unwritten laws of Heaven take precedence over the command of a mortal ruler and accepts death as the consequence. Creon orders her to be shut alive in a cave-like tomb.

l: Creon, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Creon interrogates Antigone, condemns her defiance, and insists that his authority and the State's commands must be obeyed. He rejects Ismene's attempt to share Antigone's guilt and refuses Haemon's arguments that Antigone's punishment is unjust. He orders Antigone's death by confinement in a cave-like tomb.

l: Haemon, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Haemon comes to Creon to plead for Antigone, saying that the people of Thebes mourn her and consider her burial of her brother glorious. He urges Creon to listen, change his mind, and avoid stubbornness, but leaves in deep anger after Creon refuses.

l: Ismene, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Ismene says that she will share Antigone's guilt and calamity, but Antigone refuses to let her claim responsibility for an act she did not perform. Ismene argues that life without her sister has no value and asks whether Antigone's death will also destroy Haemon's marriage.

l: Chorus of Theban Elders, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus reflects on man's power and limitations, the inherited suffering of the house of Cadmus, and the uncertainty caused by Antigone's arrest. It recognizes the force of Antigone's character, questions Creon's decision, and advises both Creon and Haemon to heed reason.

l: the Gods, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Antigone appeals to the Gods and to the eternal, unwritten laws of Heaven against Creon's mortal edict. The Chorus describes human misery as subject to divine power and says that the Gods have brought recurring calamity upon the house of Cadmus.

l: Death, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Antigone says that Death is the one fate from which man cannot obtain reprieve. She accepts death as preferable to abandoning her dead brother and describes Death as the only deity who may spare her soul in the cave-like tomb.
